newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Germany wants to send peace troops to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Germany wants to send peace troops to Bosnia.

text.p: Germany is keen to participate fully in further peacekeeping duties in Bosnia and wants to deploy troops in the former Yugoslav republic, Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said Wednesday.
Ruehe said a new international peacekeeping mandate in Bosnia to succeed that of the NATO-led peace Implementation Force (IFOR), which expires on December 20, should be limited to a year.

"It is clear there will be a new mandate and Germany will show solidarity and play a meaningful part," Ruehe told reporters in Sarajevo. "I think it should be limited to one year, but that must be discussed at a political level. This time we want to be stationed in Bosnia itself," Ruehe added.

Ruehe has made clear he wants German troops to play a full role in international peacekeeping missions after decades of avoiding military involvement abroad. Deployment of German troops to the Balkans is particularly sensitive because of their World War Two occupation of Yugoslavia.

Ruehe, speaking on arrival in Sarajevo at the start of a joint visit to German and British troops in Croatia and Bosnia with British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, said he was not pressing for a German to be in command of peacekeeping forces.
Ruehe is keen for his country's armed forces to take a more mainstream role in Bosnia if the international peacekeeping mandate is extended.
Britain has contributed a contingent of more than 9,000 to the 58,000-strong peacekeeping force. About 4,000 German support troops are based in Croatia.
Germany has said it would be prepared to contribute infantry peacekeepers with armoured vehicles to a follow-on force that could succeed IFOR.
Portillo, who arrived late on Tuesday, said he and Ruehe also wanted to assess the outcome of Bosnia's first post-war elections.

Portillo said both Britain and Germany had made "huge efforts" through the work of IFOR to implement the 1995 Dayton peace accord for Bosnia and help bring some stability to the former Yugoslav republic.
"Our task now will be to assess the outcome of the elections and how best the international community and the government of Bosnia can work together for a lasting peace," Portillo said.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic appears close to victory in the race for Bosnia's new collective presidency, with the main Serb nationalist candidate, Momcilo Krajisnik, second and the Croat, Kresimir Zubak running third.
